strengths: Well-motivated architecture (DECO) that decouples multimodal conditioning (joint self-attention for vision-action, AdaLN for proprioception, and cross-attention for tactile), matching the distinct roles and sparsity of different sensing modalities.
The plugin tactile adapter leverages parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) to successfully inject tactile capabilities into a pretrained vision-only policy, updating fewer than 10% of parameters.
Very extensive and thorough real-world evaluation, involving over 2,000 physical robot rollouts across four complex, dual-arm dexterous tasks.
Introduction and release of a large-scale, high-quality real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset (DECO-50) with high-resolution tactile feedback.
Insightful ablation studies, such as swapping the conditioning pathways, which clearly validate the importance of the specific decoupled conditioning assignments.
weaknesses: The evaluations are restricted to a single hardware setup (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire hands) and one type of tactile sensor, leaving cross-hardware generalization to future work.
While the tactile adapter is parameter-efficient, it still requires target task demonstrations with tactile data; the feasibility of zero-shot tactile adaptation remains unexplored.
Further discussion on how sensor noise or physical differences in tactile pad alignment across hands affect the robust extraction of tactile patterns would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Thorough and extensive real-world robotic evaluation with over 2,000 rollouts on a bimanual humanoid robot setup (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire dexterous hands), which is exceptionally rigorous for real-robot learning research.

A well-designed decoupled architecture (DECO) that handles multimodal inputs separately (self-attention for vision/action, AdaLN for proprioception, cross-attention for tactile). This design choice is validated through convincing ablation studies showing that swapping these conditioning pathways degrades performance.

The proposed plugin tactile adapter is parameter-efficient (<10% of trainable parameters) and offers a highly practical, modular way to inject touch sensing into pretrained vision-only policy backbones.
The release of the DECO-50 dataset (50 hours of bimanual dexterous manipulation data with tactile sensing and active vision) represents a valuable resource for the robotics research community.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to a single hardware platform with one specific type of piezoresistive tactile array. It remains unclear how easily the proposed tactile adapter generalizes to other common tactile modalities, such as high-resolution vision-based tactile sensors (e.g., GelSight or DIGIT).

While the proposed adapter uses LoRA, the paper lacks comparisons against alternative parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) structures (e.g., adapter layers, prompt tuning, or standard prefix tuning) to justify why LoRA with cross-attention is the optimal choice for tactile injection.

strengths: Extensive Real-World Robot Evaluation: Conducting over 2,000 real-world rollouts on a humanoid robot (Unitree H1-2 with dual dexterous hands) across four distinct tasks is a highly impressive physical evaluation effort.

Release of a Bimanual Tactile Dataset: The DECO-50 dataset provides 50 hours of bimanual dexterous manipulation data with active vision and dense tactile feedback (1062 taxels per hand), which represents a valuable resource for the robot learning community.

Systematic Ablation of Modality Pathways: The authors provide detailed ablation studies, including a pathway permutation test (Table 7), which convincingly shows that routing proprioceptive states through AdaLN and tactile signals through cross-attention is superior to the reverse configuration.
weaknesses: Mismatched Motivation for Parameter Efficiency (LoRA): The paper heavily emphasizes the parameter efficiency of the plugin tactile adapter using LoRA. However, the base DECO model is extremely small (83M parameters) and trained on a 50-hour dataset using 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. At this scale, training the model from scratch (89.41M parameters for DECO.ds) is computationally trivial and very fast. The parameter-efficient adapter would be highly motivated if applied to a multi-billion parameter VLA (e.g., OpenVLA, π0), but at less than 100M parameters, the absolute compute and time savings of LoRA are negligible.

Missing State-of-the-Art Visuo-Tactile Baselines: While the paper compares against general imitation learning baselines (ACT, DP, and a naive concatenation variant DP.t), it fails to compare against recent specialized visuo-tactile architectures mentioned in the related work, such as ViTacFormer (Heng et al., 2025) or Reactive Diffusion Policy (Xue et al., 2025). Without comparing against these specialized visuo-tactile baselines, it is difficult to evaluate the true performance gains of the decoupled MMDiT design.

Spatial-Agnostic Tactile Encoding: The tactile pads contain dense spatial taxel arrays (e.g., 12x8 on the finger tops). However, the tactile encoder flattens these arrays into 1D vectors and processes them with a simple 2-layer MLP and average pooling. This design discards the spatial and geometric structure of the tactile signals, which is critical for fine-grained contact localization and force vector estimation.

Unclear Contribution and Analysis of Active Vision: The active camera is highlighted as a unique feature of the dataset and setup, and the camera joints are included in the action space. However, there is no experimental analysis or ablation regarding how active vision contributes to performance, how the policy learns to control the camera, or whether a static camera setup would suffice.

strengths: Incredibly extensive real-robot evaluation with over 2,000 rollouts, which is outstanding and provides strong empirical support for the proposed method.

Release of DECO-50, a large-scale (50 hours, 8,000 trajectories) bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with dense tactile feedback (1,062 contact points per hand), representing a significant contribution to the community.

A sensible and elegant decoupled conditioning architecture (MMDiT) that separates inputs based on their roles, preventing interference and allowing for a highly parameter-efficient (less than 10% trainable parameters) tactile adapter.
Rigorous ablation studies demonstrating that the decoupled cross-attention injection performs substantially better than naive coupled concatenation or projection.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks comparisons to other recent, specialized visuo-tactile architectures (e.g., ViTacFormer or slow-fast models), as the baselines are limited to ACT, standard DP, and a basic concatenation variant (DP.t).

The framework is evaluated entirely on a specific hardware platform (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire hands), and the paper would benefit from a discussion on how the tactile adapter can generalize to other tactile sensors like GelSight or DIGIT.
The absence of a simulated benchmark or simulator setup makes it challenging for other research groups without identical hardware to reproduce, validate, or build directly upon the physical results.

strengths: Highly practical and parameter-efficient architecture: The decoupled design (joint self-attention for vision-action, AdaLN for proprioception, and cross-attention with LoRA for tactile) enables modular and cost-effective expansion of pre-trained policies, requiring training of less than 10% of total parameters.

Outstanding real-world evaluation: Conducting over 2,000 physical robot rollouts across multiple complex contact-rich tasks (such as assembly and waste disposal with diverse objects and sizes) provides exceptionally rigorous empirical evidence of the method's effectiveness.

Valuable dataset release: The DECO-50 dataset provides 50 hours (over 5M frames, 8K trajectories) of bimanual dexterous manipulation data equipped with multi-point tactile sensing (1,062 contact points per hand), addressing a major resource bottleneck in the community.

Strong baseline comparison and ablation: The experiments systematically compare against standard architectures (ACT, Diffusion Policy) and thoroughly ablate coupled versus decoupled tactile fusion schemes, showing clear advantages for the decoupled approach.
weaknesses: Limited exploration of tactile sensor diversity: The design and evaluation are customized around the Inspire hand's low-dimensional tactile grid (17 pads). It remains unclear how well the simple average-pooling tactile encoder scales to high-resolution optical tactile sensors (e.g., GelSight, DIGIT) which behave more like dense images.

Simplistic temporal modeling: The policy models actions over short chunks without a long-term temporal sequence memory (e.g., a transformer state history), which may limit its robustness in complex, long-horizon tasks requiring explicit state tracking over time.

strengths: Extensive real-world evaluation: Conducting over 2,000 real-world robot rollouts across four complex, multi-stage tasks is a highly impressive feat that far exceeds the evaluation scale of typical robotic learning papers.

Significant dataset contribution (DECO-50): Releasing a 50-hour bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with 5 million frames, 8,000 successful trajectories, and high-density tactile sensing (1,062 contact points) is a valuable contribution to the robotics community.

Well-motivated architecture design: The decoupled multimodal DiT (MMDiT) separates different sensor modalities based on their physical characteristics (joint self-attention for vision-action, AdaLN for proprioception, and cross-attention/LoRA for sparse tactile signals), preventing mutual interference.

Highly parameter-efficient adaptation: The two-stage training paradigm with a plugin tactile adapter allows adding tactile capabilities to a pretrained vision-action policy by training less than 10% of the parameters, achieving comparable performance to training from scratch.

Clear presentation and thorough ablation studies: The paper is exceptionally well-written, with highly informative figures and rigorous ablation studies (e.g., comparing coupled vs. decoupled injection in Table 5).
weaknesses: Lack of state-of-the-art visuo-tactile baselines: While the authors compare against ACT, DP, and DP with tactile concatenation (DP.t), they do not benchmark against more advanced, recent visuo-tactile fusion methods mentioned in the related work (such as ViTacFormer or slow-fast temporal architectures).

Ambiguity regarding active vision: The paper mentions an 'active camera' and includes its proprioceptive joint states in the observation. However, it is not clear whether the policy actively controls the camera's yaw and pitch joints (i.e., active perception) or if the camera motion is predetermined/teleoperated.

No simulation environment: Since real bimanual dexterous setups with rich tactile sensing are extremely expensive and difficult to replicate, the absence of a simulated counterpart makes it hard for other researchers without this hardware to reproduce, benchmark, and build upon the work.

strengths: Outstanding and highly extensive real-world robot evaluation with over 2,000 rollouts across four distinct bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
Release of DECO-50, a significant, large-scale (50 hours, 5M frames, 8K successful trajectories) bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with rich tactile feedback and active vision.

A well-designed, decoupled conditioning architecture that respects the nature of different modalities (e.g., vision/action via self-attention, proprioception via global AdaLN, and sparse tactile via localized cross-attention).
Highly parameter-efficient second-stage training via the plugin tactile adapter, tuning under 10% of the parameters while enabling a 20% performance boost on contact-rich tasks.
Rigorous and informative ablation studies, particularly the pathway swap experiment that confirms why the chosen modality-to-pathway mapping is crucial.
weaknesses: The architectural components (DiT, AdaLN, cross-attention, LoRA) are individually standard; the methodological novelty is largely in the integration and robot-specific configuration rather than brand-new architecture design.

The tactile encoder design and raw-value processing seem somewhat tailored to the specific Inspire RH56DFTP hand with piezoresistive sensors. The paper would benefit from a discussion on how generalizable this adapter is to other tactile modalities (e.g., camera-based tactile sensors like GelSight).
The role and control of 'active vision' (the active camera's yaw and pitch joints) are mentioned but not extensively discussed or analyzed in the main text.

strengths: Highly thorough and impressive real-world evaluation, involving over 2,000 real robot rollouts across diverse tasks, which is exceptionally rigorous and rare for robot learning publications.

Release of the DECO-50 dataset, a large-scale (50 hours, 5M frames, 8K trajectories) bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset featuring dense tactile feedback (1,062 contact points per hand), which fills a critical gap in the visuo-tactile bimanual research community.

The proposed two-stage training strategy with a plugin tactile adapter and LoRA fine-tuning is highly practical, allowing pre-trained vision-action models to be adapted to tactile-rich tasks by tuning less than 10% of the parameters.

Excellent ablation studies, specifically the conditioning pathway permutation experiment (Table 7), which clearly justifies why local/fine-grained tactile signals are suited for cross-attention, while global joint states are better suited for AdaLN.

Extensive simulation results across four distinct benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, and DexJoCo) demonstrate the model's generality and superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
weaknesses: While the multimodal decoupling and parameter-efficient adapter are highly effective, the architectural components themselves (such as MMDiT, AdaLN, cross-attention, and LoRA) are well-established, making the methodological novelty somewhat evolutionary rather than revolutionary.

The paper frequently mentions 'active vision' and 'active camera joints' in the text, but the exact mechanism for controlling the active camera during inference is not fully detailed. It is somewhat unclear if the camera's yaw/pitch motion is actively controlled by the policy as part of the action space or pre-programmed.

The real-world validation, while extensive, is constrained to a single dual-arm platform (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire hands), meaning the cross-hardware generalization of the tactile adapter to different tactile layouts or hands is yet to be demonstrated.

strengths: Highly impressive and extensive real-world robot evaluation with over 2,000 rollouts on a complex dual-arm dexterous manipulation platform (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire hands).

The release of DECO-50, a large-scale (50 hours, 5M frames, 8K trajectories) real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with dense tactile sensing, addressing a major resource bottleneck in the community.

A well-reasoned, decoupled conditioning architecture (MMDiT) that sensibly aligns the bandwidth and spatial-temporal characteristics of different modalities with appropriate fusion mechanisms (joint self-attention, AdaLN, and cross-attention).

An effective parameter-efficient tactile adapter showing how tactile signals can be successfully injected into a frozen, pre-trained vision-action policy while training fewer than 10% of the parameters.

Exceptionally thorough evaluations and ablation studies, including a pathway permutation test and extensive simulation evaluations on four distinct benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, DexJoCo).
weaknesses: The individual architectural components (DiT, AdaLN, LoRA, cross-attention) are standard and well-established; the novelty primarily lies in their combination and specific routing design for multimodal robot policies.

The high complexity and cost of the custom hardware platform (humanoid robot, 1062-taxel dexterous hands, active binocular camera, and Vision Pro teleoperation) may limit direct real-world physical reproduction in smaller academic labs.

The tactile sensors are primarily used for contact/state detection rather than continuous, high-frequency closed-loop force/torque control, leaving some aspects of dynamic force regulation unaddressed.
